lessons.title: One league, one table
lessons.objective: You can explain how the league table decides the champion.

payload.prompt: How many points does a team get for a league win?

options.text: One point
Two points
Three points

explanation.correct: Right. A win is three points, a draw is one, and a loss is zero. The table is sorted by points first.
explanation.incorrect: It's three points for a win. That's why you hear fans say a draw feels like a loss when chasing the title.
explanation.sayThisLine: A draw's like a loss when you're fighting for the title.

payload.prompt: Two teams have the same points. What breaks the tie first?

options.text: Head-to-head record
Goal difference
Alphabetical order

explanation.correct: Right. Goal difference (goals scored minus goals conceded) is the first tiebreaker in most leagues. Then it's goals scored.
explanation.incorrect: It's goal difference. That's why fans say 'We're level on points but their goal difference is better.'
explanation.sayThisLine: We're level on points but their goal difference is better.

payload.prompt: Complete the league points system.
payload.template: A win is {{win}} points, a draw is {{draw}} point, and a loss is {{loss}} points.

explanation.correct: Right. Three for a win, one for a draw, zero for a loss. The league is decided by total points.
explanation.incorrect: The system is three, one, zero. That makes wins valuable and draws less so.

payload.prompt: Who wins the league?

options.text: The team with the most wins
The team with the most points
The team with the best goal difference

explanation.correct: Right. The team with the most points wins, even if they have fewer wins than someone else (because draws count).
explanation.incorrect: It's the most points. A team could have fewer wins but more draws and still have more points.

payload.prompt: A 1-1 draw feels how to fans chasing the title?

options.text: Like a win
Like a draw
Like a loss

explanation.correct: Right. One point from a draw hurts when you're trying to win the league; fans would rather take three.
explanation.incorrect: A draw is technically a point, but when you're hunting the title, it feels like dropping two points.

lessons.title: Going up and going down
lessons.objective: You can explain promotion and relegation.

payload.prompt: What happens to the worst teams in most world leagues?

options.text: They stay in the league but lose money
They get relegated to a lower division
They have to buy better players

explanation.correct: Right. Relegation drops the bottom teams down a division. It's why fans get nervous; there's real danger.
explanation.incorrect: In most of the world, the worst teams drop down to a lower division. That's called relegation, and it's brutal.

payload.prompt: Where do the promoted teams come from?

options.text: The top of the league below
A draft
The previous season's runners-up

explanation.correct: Right. The top teams from the division below get promoted up. It's a ladder system.
explanation.incorrect: Promotion comes from the division below. The best teams down there go up; the worst teams here go down.

payload.prompt: Why does relegation make the league exciting?

options.text: Because teams fight hard to avoid it
Because it is always entertaining
Because promoted teams always win

explanation.correct: Right. Relegation means real stakes. The bottom teams play with their lives on the line; it's dramatic.
explanation.incorrect: Relegation is a threat, so every match matters, especially at the bottom. That's what makes the race brutal.

payload.fanLine: Three go down and it gets brutal at the bottom.

replies.text: Right, so the bottom three get relegated? That must put pressure on every team near the bottom.

replies.coachNote: Honest question shows you are learning.

payload.prompt: True or false: MLS has relegation like Premier League does.

options.text: True, teams drop leagues
False, there's no relegation in MLS

explanation.correct: Right. MLS is different; there's no relegation, so no matter how bad you are, you stay in the top league.
explanation.incorrect: MLS has no relegation. It's a single-entity league with a salary cap, so the worst team stays in MLS.

lessons.title: Domestic cups
lessons.objective: You can explain why the cup produces upsets.

payload.prompt: What is a domestic cup?

options.text: A knockout tournament inside one country where small clubs face giants
A league for smaller teams
A trophy for the best defensive team

explanation.correct: Right. The cup (like the FA Cup or Copa del Rey) is a knockout, so any team can beat any other team in one match.
explanation.incorrect: A domestic cup is a knockout tournament inside one country. Small clubs face giants, and that's where upsets happen.

payload.prompt: Why do small teams have a chance to beat big teams in the cup?

options.text: Because it's one match, not a season-long series
Because big teams don't play their best players
Because small teams get extra players

explanation.correct: Right. A single match is a lottery; anyone can win one night. In the league, form and strength over 38 games decide it.
explanation.incorrect: It's the knockout format. One match means anything can happen. The best league finisher might not win the cup.

payload.prompt: How does a domestic cup bracket usually work?

options.text: Round-robin, everyone plays each other
Knockout, lose once and you are out
Best-of-three series

explanation.correct: Right. Knockout means one loss and you go home. That's where the magic is; one bad day and it's over.
explanation.incorrect: A cup is knockout. One match, one winner. That's why small clubs dream of beating giants.

payload.fanLine: It's the cup, so anything can happen.

replies.text: Right, one-off match, so even a small team has a shot?
replies.coachNote: Shows you understand why upsets happen.

payload.prompt: Why do fans talk about 'cup magic' or 'cup runs'?

options.text: Because smaller teams sometimes beat giants in knockout football
Because the cup has better players
Because it's played at night

explanation.correct: Right. A cup run is when a smaller team keeps winning and makes a deep run. It's the romance of the cup.
explanation.incorrect: Cup magic is a small team beating a giant. The knockout format means one match changes everything.

lessons.title: Europe and qualification
lessons.objective: You can explain how a club qualifies for the Champions League.

payload.prompt: How do clubs get into European competitions like the Champions League?

options.text: They win a domestic cup
They finish high enough in their league
They are invited by UEFA

explanation.correct: Right. League position is the main path. Finishing in the top spots (usually top four) qualifies you for the Champions League.
explanation.incorrect: It's mainly league position. If you finish in the top four or so, you get Champions League football next season.

payload.prompt: Match the European competition to its rank.

pairs.definition: The top European club competition; mainly for the best league finishers
The second-tier European competition for mid-table finishers and cup winners

explanation.correct: Right. Champions League is the prize. Europa League is the consolation. Conference League is the entry-level European night.
explanation.incorrect: The pyramid is Champions League (best teams), Europa League (next level), then Conference League (entry level).

payload.prompt: Why do fans say 'We need top four for Champions League'?

options.text: Because finishing top four in the league qualifies you
Because there are only four teams in Europe
Because the rule changes every year

explanation.correct: Right. Most domestic leagues use top four (or top six or eight depending on the league) to qualify for the Champions League.
explanation.incorrect: It's a league position thing. Finish high enough and you get European football next season, which means more matches, more prize money, more prestige.

payload.prompt: Can a domestic cup winner get into European football even if they finish low in the league?

options.text: Yes, some leagues give cup winners a European spot
No, you have to finish high in the league
It depends on the cup

explanation.correct: Right. In many leagues, if you win the domestic cup, you get a Europa League spot even if you finished mid-table.
explanation.incorrect: Cup winners often get a European spot. It's an extra reward for winning the cup.

payload.prompt: When fans say 'We're fighting for Europe', what do they mean?

options.text: They are trying to finish high enough to qualify for European competitions
They are playing teams from Europe
They are moving to Europe

explanation.correct: Right. European football is a big deal: more prestige, more revenue, more matches and a bigger stage.
explanation.incorrect: Fighting for Europe means trying to qualify for Champions League or Europa League by finishing high in the league.

lessons.title: Transfers, loans and contracts
lessons.objective: You can explain a loan, a fee and a free transfer.

payload.prompt: Match the transfer term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: The price a club pays for a player's contract
Borrowing a player from another club for one season
A player moving for no fee because his contract has expired

explanation.correct: Right. Fee = money, loan = temporary, free = contract expired. Those are the three ways a player moves.
explanation.incorrect: A fee is money paid for a contract. A loan is temporary. Free means the contract ended, so no fee.

payload.prompt: When can clubs sign new players?

options.text: Only during the transfer window, usually summer and January
Anytime during the season
Only before the season starts

explanation.correct: Right. The transfer window is a fixed period. Summer is the big one; January is the small one.
explanation.incorrect: The window opens and closes. Clubs can only register players during those periods.

payload.scenario: A young player wants more playing time but his club won't give it to him. What do clubs usually do?

options.text: Loan him to a smaller club to get experience
options.explanation: Right. Loans let young players develop elsewhere and come back better.

options.text: Sell him immediately
options.explanation: They could, but a loan is smarter; if he develops well, they get him back.

options.text: Keep him on the bench
options.explanation: That wastes his potential. A loan lets him develop and come back.

payload.prompt: A player's contract expires this summer. What can happen?

options.text: He can negotiate with any club and leave for free
His club can force him to stay
He has to pay to leave

explanation.correct: Right. In the last months of a contract, a player can talk to other clubs and leave for free when it ends.
explanation.incorrect: Contract expiry means freedom. When the contract ends, the player goes free; his old club gets nothing.

payload.prompt: He's on loan with an option to buy. What does that mean?

options.text: The borrowing club can decide to buy his contract at a set price
The player can choose to leave anytime
The original club has to sell him

explanation.correct: Right. An option to buy lets the loaning club decide later whether to make it permanent, at a pre-agreed price.
explanation.incorrect: Option to buy means the loaning club has a choice. If the player shines, they can trigger it.

lessons.title: Academy and the club machine
lessons.objective: You can explain the roles of manager, academy and sporting director.

payload.prompt: What is a club's academy?

options.text: A youth system that develops young players who might reach the first team
A school for fans
A training facility for retired players

explanation.correct: Right. The academy brings in kids, trains them, and either sells them or promotes them to the first team.
explanation.incorrect: An academy is the youth system. You hear fans say a player 'came through the academy' when he rose from the youth teams.

payload.prompt: What does a manager do?

options.text: Picks the team and decides tactics
Buys and sells players
Owns the club

explanation.correct: Right. The manager is the head coach; he picks the starting eleven and decides how the team plays.
explanation.incorrect: The manager is the tactical boss. He picks the team and the formation every match.

payload.prompt: What does the sporting director do?

options.text: Runs recruitment and long-term planning
Picks the team for each match
Owns the stadium

explanation.correct: Right. The sporting director (or head of football) buys, sells and plans the squad's future.
explanation.incorrect: The sporting director is the architect. He runs transfers and squad planning; the manager works with what he builds.

payload.fanLine: The manager wanted him but the sporting director wouldn't pay the fee.

replies.text: So they disagreed on the transfer? That happens, I guess.
replies.coachNote: Shows you understand the power split.

replies.text: What's the difference between those two?
They should have bought him anyway.
replies.coachNote: Easy to say, but budgets matter.

payload.prompt: When fans say a player is a 'local lad', what do they often mean?

options.text: He came through the academy and grew up at the club
He was born nearby
He is cheap

explanation.correct: Right. A local product is someone who rose through the academy. Fans love it; it means loyalty.
explanation.incorrect: He came through the academy' usually means a homegrown player. Fans celebrate those because they are club-made.

lessons.title: Derbies and matchday culture
lessons.objective: You can explain why derbies, supporter culture and spending rules matter.

payload.prompt: What is a derby?

options.text: A match between local rivals with deep history
A cup competition
An international tournament

explanation.correct: Right. A derby is more than three points; it's pride, history and local bragging rights.
explanation.incorrect: A derby is a local rivalry match. The form book goes out the window; anything can happen when neighbours play.

payload.prompt: Why do derbies often produce upset results?

options.text: Because emotion and pride override form; weaker teams raise their game
Because the pitch is smaller
Because the referee favours local teams

explanation.correct: Right. A derby is emotional; the underdog brings everything, and form counts for less.
explanation.incorrect: Derbies are about pride. A weaker team can play out of their skin against local rivals.

payload.prompt: What are supporters' groups?

options.text: Chants, banners and fan organisations that create the atmosphere
VIP members who get free tickets
The club's owners

explanation.correct: Right. Ultras and supporters' trusts drive the noise and culture. They are the soul of matchday.
explanation.incorrect: Supporters' culture includes chants, banners (tifo), and organized fan groups. They create the atmosphere and identity.

payload.prompt: Why do leagues have spending rules?

options.text: To prevent rich clubs from dominating too completely
To make everyone equal
To reduce player salaries

explanation.correct: Right. Spending rules try to keep competition fair. Too much money too fast breaks the league.
explanation.incorrect: Rules like the Premier League's squad-cost limit and UEFA's squad cost ratio try to prevent unlimited spending from warping competition.

payload.fanLine: It's a derby, throw the form book out.

replies.text: So the weaker team has a real shot because emotion matters more than usual?
replies.coachNote: Shows you understand why derbies are unpredictable.

replies.text: What do you mean by the form book?
So your team will definitely win?
